clinicalPearls: A condition with the physical features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy but normal calcium and normal parathyroid hormone responsiveness
Features of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy include short stature, a round face, brachydactyly (notably short fourth metacarpals) and subcutaneous ossifications
Unlike pseudohypoparathyroidism, there is no hormone resistance and biochemistry is normal
It is caused by GNAS mutations inherited from the father, whereas maternal inheritance of the same mutation causes pseudohypoparathyroidism (an example of imprinting)
It sits within the same family as pseudohypoparathyroidism and is distinguished biochemically
Management is mainly of the skeletal and cosmetic features, with genetic counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism arises from a heterozygous inactivating GNAS mutation affecting the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein. Because GNAS is imprinted, the phenotype depends on the parent of origin: paternal transmission produces the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy physical phenotype without hormone resistance (pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism), whereas maternal transmission additionally causes resistance to parathyroid hormone and other hormones (pseudohypoparathyroidism) because the maternal allele is the active one in key tissues. Hence calcium and parathyroid hormone signalling are normal here despite the shared skeletal features.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of brachydactyly or short stature
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate and parathyroid hormone (normal)
Assessment of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features
GNAS genetic testing and parent-of-origin assessment
redFlags: Biochemical hormone resistance, which would indicate pseudohypoparathyroidism instead
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign biochemically, and prognosis relates to the skeletal and cosmetic features rather than to calcium disturbance.
pitfalls: Confusing it with pseudohypoparathyroidism despite normal biochemistry
Overlooking the imprinting/parent-of-origin basis in counselling
Missing the diagnosis in a relative of a pseudohypoparathyroidism patient
management: Reassure and withhold calcium and vitamin D therapy, as calcium and parathyroid hormone signalling are normal here unlike in pseudohypoparathyroidism
Symptomatic orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features, with excision of troublesome subcutaneous ossifications
Hand therapy and selective orthopaedic input for brachydactyly, short metacarpals and functional hand problems
Confirm the diagnosis with GNAS testing and parent-of-origin assessment to distinguish it from pseudohypoparathyroidism
Periodic clinical and biochemical review to ensure hormone resistance does not emerge

Genetic counselling on autosomal dominant imprinted inheritance, explaining that paternal transmission produces this phenotype whereas maternal transmission causes pseudohypoparathyroidism, with family screening
Multidisciplinary input from clinical genetics, endocrinology and orthopaedics
